canManage() is granted by the VIEW scope, so a view-only all-groups permission lets the admin create groups

`canManage()` returns `hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)`, so any `view` permission on the Groups resource type makes it true. `GroupsResource` guards creating a top-level group with `auth.groups().requireManage()` (GroupsResource.java:181). The result: an admin who was only given `view` on all groups can create top-level groups (and anything else gated on `canManage()`). Every other manage check in this class asks only for MANAGE (`canManage(GroupModel)` at line 79), and so does V1 `canManage()` (GroupPermissions.java:275). Change it to `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`, and fix the interface Javadoc (GroupPermissionEvaluator.java:75-76), which describes the same wrong rule. `testManageAllGroups` only grants MANAGE, so this case is never tested.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses the resource's id where the group id (the resource name) is needed

V2 group resources are named after the group id, and their own id is generated: `getOrCreateResource` calls `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, ...)` with `name = group.getId()` (AdminPermissionsSchema.java:118-121, 185). This loop passes `groupResource.getId()` to `hasPermission`, which calls `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` (line 141). That lookup never matches, so evaluation falls back to the all-groups resource. The loop then also adds resource ids to `granted`. That set is used as group ids for `session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, ...)` (UsersResource.java:448-450, BruteForceUsersResource.java:147-149) and for `getUsersCount(realm, ..., groupIds)` (UsersResource.java:398/425/430). An admin with per-group VIEW_MEMBERS then gets the wrong user count, and the search is filtered by group ids that do not exist, with no error. The sibling `ClientPermissionsV2.getClientsWithPermission` uses `resource.getName()` (ClientPermissionsV2.java:138-140). Use `groupResource.getName()` in both places.

VIEW_MEMBERS tests never check users/count or the group-id filter

`testCanViewUserByViewGroupMembers` only checks the user search. That search still passes when `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission` returns wrong ids, because `toRepresentation` filters each user with `canView` again (UsersResource.java:460). Asserting `users().count()` for myadmin after granting VIEW_MEMBERS would catch the id/name mismatch at GroupPermissionsV2.java:122. A test that grants only `view` on all groups and then expects group creation to be FORBIDDEN would catch the `canManage()` scope bug.

requireManageMembers Javadoc points to the wrong method

The Javadoc says it throws when `canManageMembership(GroupModel)` is false, but the implementations check `canManageMembers` (GroupPermissions.java:376-379). Also, the `@return` at line 145 says "Stream of IDs", but the method returns a `Set`.

Removing the multiple-provider check lets a FIPS/non-FIPS mix on the classpath pick a provider silently

Before this change, `detectProvider` threw `IllegalStateException` when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found. Now it sorts by `order()` and takes the first one. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200 (DefaultCryptoProvider.java:83-85, WildFlyElytronProvider.java:76-78, FIPS1402Provider.java:114-116). When two of them are on the classpath, the stable sort keeps ServiceLoader (classpath) order, and the losers are logged only at debug level (lines 64-70). So a deployment that has both `keycloak-crypto-default` and `keycloak-crypto-fips1402` used to fail at startup. Now it can quietly run on the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider, and nothing at default log levels says so. This affects every caller of `CryptoIntegration.init`: `KeycloakApplication.startup()` (services/.../KeycloakApplication.java:89), the admin CLI (`Globals.java:44`) and the testsuite `CryptoInitRule`. The Quarkus server is not affected because it calls `setProvider` explicitly (KeycloakRecorder.java:214). The new ordering only needs a fallback provider to lose against the real ones. Keep the fail-fast when two or more providers share the top `order()` value, and throw the same message as before.

One default-size EC key is used for ES256, ES384 and ES512, so the round trip compares truncated values

`KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` makes one key on the JDK's default curve (P-256 on older JDKs, P-384 on newer ones), and all three tests use it. When the key's r/s are longer than `signLength/2` (for example a P-384 key under ES256, where r/s are up to 48 bytes and `len` is 32), `integerToBytes` (AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:153-156) silently keeps only the last `len` bytes. `rsConcat` and `rsConcat2` are then both truncated the same way, so `assertArrayEquals` passes on a signature that cannot be valid. ES512 is never tested with a P-521 key either. The test can't catch a bug in the length handling. Generate a key per algorithm (`initialize(new ECGenParameterSpec("secp256r1"/"secp384r1"/"secp521r1"))`). Also check that `asn1Des` verifies with `Signature.verify` against the public key, or equals the original `sign`, instead of only checking that the round trip is self-consistent.

Two encoder calls build objects that are never used

Lines 114-115 (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger)` and the same for `s`) build encoders and throw them away. The returned sequence builds its own encoders on lines 119-120. Remove both lines.

Reader thread is never joined, so the test can pass without checking anything

The reader thread starts at line 139 and nothing waits for it. Line 155 sets `deletedAll` and line 157 asserts right away. Two things go wrong:
- A request that is still running when the deletes finish can add its exception after the assertion has already run. The test then passes even though the race happened, and the stray thread keeps using `managedRealm.admin()` while the next test runs.
- Nothing checks that the reader made any request while deletes were happening. If the thread is slow to start, the test passes without testing the race at all.

Also, `catch (Exception e)` misses `Error`s (for example an `AssertionError`), and those die silently with the thread.

Fix: keep a reference to the `Thread`, call `join()` (with a timeout) after line 155, count completed reads with an `AtomicInteger` and assert the count is > 0, and catch `Throwable`.

The three sibling `getSubGroupsStream` overloads have the same null dereference

`getSubGroupsCount` now handles `modelSupplier.get()` returning null when the group was deleted after it was cached. The overloads at lines 256, 262 and 268 still call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` directly, so a concurrent delete gives the same NPE there. `GroupResource.getSubGroups` reaches this through `group.getSubGroupsStream(search, exact, -1, -1)` (services/.../GroupResource.java:180). These are probably less exposed, because the resource looks the group up first, but the race window is the same. Consider applying the same guard, or throwing `NotFound`, in all four methods.

A deleted group is still returned in the list, now with `subGroupCount: null`

When the database row is gone, `getSubGroupsCount()` now returns null. `GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount` stores that null in the representation (GroupUtils.java:90), and `GroupsResource.getGroups` returns the group in the listing (GroupsResource.java:120-125). The NPE is gone, but a client gets a just-deleted group whose `subGroupCount` is null, while every other entry has a number. The admin UI and clients that treat the field as always present may break on it. Consider filtering such groups out of the stream in `GroupsResource`/`GroupUtils`, or returning `0L`, so the list stays consistent.

Call to `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments does not compile

`UsernameForm.authenticate` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only definition is `UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` (UsernamePasswordForm.java:160). A repository-wide search finds no zero-argument overload in `UsernamePasswordForm`, `AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator` or anywhere else, so the `services` module fails to compile. Pass the user: `!isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`.

`user != null` turns passkeys off on normal login and turns them on only for re-authentication

Before this change, the passkey (conditional UI) data was filled only when no user was set yet: in the `else` branch of `authenticate`, and under `context.getUser() == null` in `challenge`. The new helper requires `user != null`, so the condition is now the reverse:
- On a first login (`context.getUser()` is null), `authenticate` (line 115) no longer calls `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm`. The username/password page then has no challenge and no `ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI`, so passwordless login through the default browser flow stops working.
- `challenge(...)` (line 137) drops passkeys after an unknown username, because `testInvalidUser` calls it with a null user (AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator.java:105-111).

The PR's own tests expect the passkey form on the first login page (PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.java:196 and 238, `//form[@id='webauth']`), so they would fail.

The intended condition is probably `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && (user == null || user.credentialManager().isConfiguredFor(webauthnAuth.getCredentialType()))`. That keeps passkeys on the anonymous login page and shows them during re-authentication only to users who actually have a passkey.

`reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` turns passkeys off for the realm, so it never tests a user without a passkey

The test sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE)`, so the passkey UI is hidden whatever credentials the user has. The comment at line 304 ("as this user does not have passkey") describes a case the test never reaches: passkeys enabled for the realm, re-authenticating a user who has only a password. That is the case the logic above gets wrong. Enable passkeys for the realm here and assert that `//form[@id='webauth']` is missing. Also, the `try { assertThat(..., nullValue()); fail(...) } catch (Exception)` pattern (lines 291-296 and 312-317) only works because `AssertionError` is not an `Exception`. `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...)`, as used in PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest, states the intent directly.

Hung flusher process is never killed before it is replaced

In production, processes are created with `self.mp_context.Process` (line 105), where `mp_context` is `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")` (line 53). That makes them `SpawnProcess` objects. `SpawnProcess` inherits from `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, not from `multiprocessing.Process`, so `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False and `process.kill()` never runs.

The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. Now, on a `hang`, line 259 starts a second process on the same shards while the hung one is still alive. That has three effects:
- Both processes read the same Redis queues, so segments can be flushed and produced twice.
- The hung process still writes to the same shared `healthy_since`/`backpressure_since` Values.
- Each restart leaks one process, because `self.processes[process_index]` is overwritten and `join` no longer sees the old one.

Fix: test `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)` (or `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`). Line 346 in `join` has the same check, so `terminate()` never runs there either. That check was there before this PR, but it is worth fixing in the same change.

`join` skips terminate for every process left once the deadline passes

When the deadline has passed, the loop does `break`. Every process not yet visited is then neither waited for nor terminated. The old code always reached the terminate step after its wait. To keep the deadline as a bound on waiting without dropping the cleanup, skip only the wait (for example, compute `remaining_time` and skip the `while` when it is not positive) and still call terminate on every process. This matters once the isinstance check at line 346 is fixed. Until then, terminate never runs for spawn processes at all.

Per-process buffers multiply the `max-flush-segments` budget and loosen the backpressure threshold

`SpansBuffer.flush_segments` divides `spans.buffer.max-flush-segments` by `len(self.assigned_shards)` (src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:382-384). Each shard buffer now holds only its process's shards. With N processes, each shard's per-iteration limit, and so the total flushed per cycle, grows by N. The `any_shard_at_limit` backpressure threshold (buffer.py:411-412) is per-shard too, so it rises by the same factor. If this is the intended throughput gain, say so in the PR description or in the option's description. Otherwise, divide the option by the total shard count.

Redis memory info is fetched once per flusher buffer on every submit

`get_memory_info` calls `iter_cluster_memory_usage(self.client)`. `client` is the same `get_redis_client()` for every buffer (src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:161-163, 375-376). This loop therefore queries the whole cluster N times per `submit` and sums each node N times. The ratio comes out the same, but it costs N× the INFO calls. Calling it once (for example on the first buffer) gives the same result. `record_stored_segments` (line 269-270) also goes from one pipeline to N.

Dead code: `_create_process_for_shard` and the `if not process` guard

Nothing calls `_create_process_for_shard`; a search of the repository finds only its definition. The `if not process: continue` guard at line 222 can never fire, because `self.processes` only ever holds started Process/Thread objects (line 124). Both can be removed.

Docstring says one process per shard, but the CLI default is a single process

`--flusher-processes` defaults to 1 (src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py:432-437), and shards are spread round-robin over `min(max_processes, len(shards))` processes (lines 60-66). The class docstring should describe that instead of "one process per shard". The comments at line 178 ("for all shards") and line 235 ("if any shard ... is unhealthy") also describe per-shard checks, but the value they refer to is a single per-process value.

Inconsistent metric tag key: `shards` vs `shard`

`spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged `shards`, but `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `segment_size_bytes` are tagged `shard` with the same `shard_tag` value (lines 185, 195). Use one key so dashboards can group these metrics together.

`time.sleep(0.1)` does nothing, because `time.sleep` is monkeypatched at line 15

`monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` replaces `time.sleep` globally, so this call returns at once and the comment "Give flusher threads time to process" is false. The test actually depends on `step.join()` busy-waiting until the threads exit. Remove the sleep, or wait on a condition (for example, poll until `messages` is not empty with a bounded loop).

New tests don't cover shard ownership or the restart/kill path

`test_flusher_processes_limit` only checks counts. It doesn't check that each process flushes only its own shards, or that segments from all 4 partitions are produced. Nothing tests `_ensure_processes_alive`, so the kill regression at flusher.py:254 goes unnoticed. A test that marks one process unhealthy, by setting its `process_healthy_since` value into the past, and then asserts the old process is gone would catch it.

zip(error_ids, events.values()) can attach error data to the wrong ID

`nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node ID. It dedupes the input, and when some IDs are cached and others are not, it builds the result from a cache dict plus an uncached dict (src/sentry/nodestore/base.py:183-204). So the order of `.values()` is not guaranteed to match `error_ids`, and duplicate error IDs make the lengths differ. Zipping by position can then pair the wrong `id` with the wrong title, message and timestamp. Look each one up by key instead: `events.get(node_id)` for every `(event_id, node_id)` pair.

Error timestamps (seconds) are compared with replay event timestamps (milliseconds)

An error's `timestamp` comes from nodestore event data, which stores epoch seconds as a float. Replay recording events (rrweb) carry epoch milliseconds in `timestamp`. A seconds value is always smaller than a milliseconds value, so the `while` loop emits every error before the first breadcrumb and the intended chronological interleaving never happens. The summary Seer receives is then silently out of order. Convert one side, e.g. compare `error['timestamp'] * 1000` with `event.get('timestamp', 0)`, and add a test that uses realistic units.

get_environment_info runs one recommended-event lookup per issue

Both the GitHub and GitLab merged-PR comment builders now call `get_environment_info` for every issue in the list. Each call runs `issue.get_recommended_event()`, which is an eventstore/Snuba query, and then `get_environment()`. That makes the comment task N+1 over the issue list. The list is small today, but batching the lookups or reading environment data from the issues query that already exists would avoid the extra round-trips.

Analytics event is recorded before the feature-flag check

`preprod_artifact.api.assemble` is recorded before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` check. Requests that are then rejected with 404 still count as assemble calls, which inflates the metric. If the goal is to measure real usage, move the record call after the feature check, or add an attribute that marks rejected calls.

With the feature flag on, table widgets always render empty

When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, `TableWidgetVisualization` gets `columns={[]}` and empty `tableData`. `tableResults`, `loading` and the field renderers are all ignored. Any org with the flag sees every table widget empty, with no data and no loading state. If this is a placeholder, keep the flag off for every org until real data is passed through.

Boolean(normalizedDateRange) is always true

`normalizeDateTimeParams` returns an object, so `Boolean(normalizedDateRange)` is always `true` and does not gate the query. Either drop the condition or check the field the code actually depends on, e.g. that `start`/`end` or `statsPeriod` is present.

Hidden attributes still show when the search box is empty

The `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` check only runs inside the search filter (lines 65-69). When `searchQuery.trim()` is empty, the early return at lines 61-63 hands back `sorted` as is, so `is_segment`, `project_id` and `received` still appear in the default view, which is the view most users see. They only disappear once the user types something. Apply the hidden filter to `sorted` before the early return, for example `const sorted = sortAttributes(attributes).filter(a => !HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(a.name));`.

Attribute-keys query no longer sends the selected environments

Before this change, `useTraceItemAttributeKeys` sent `environment: selection.environments` to `/trace-items/attributes/`. The shared `makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions` now leaves it out, with the comment "environment left out intentionally as it's not supported". As a result, the attribute suggestions in Explore and Logs no longer follow the environment page filter. Does the endpoint really ignore `environment`? If it doesn't, users with an environment selected will now get keys from every environment.

Query options from the old `useApiQuery` were dropped

The old query passed `staleTime: 0, refetchOnWindowFocus: false, retry: false`. The new `useQuery` call passes none of these, so the client defaults now apply: failures may be retried, and the query may refetch when the window regains focus. Because `isLoading` now maps to `isFetching` (line 61), every background refetch also flips the search bar's attributes into the loading state. If the old behaviour was wanted, add those options back.

Typo and missing space in story text "Below is the the most basic example" repeats "the". There is also no space between "requires" and `tableData`, and the same happens at line 57 before `TabularData` and at line 110 before `renderTableBodyCell`. All of these render as run-together words.

Renamed class says "Spans" but its fixtures are error and transaction events

The class is now called `OrganizationEventsStatsTopNEventsSpans`, but its `setUp` stores error events (`message`/`fingerprint`) and a `load_data("transaction")` event through the discover path (lines 1260-1309). It does not set up span data. The new logs test's comment (line 3087, "implemented almost exactly the same as spans") repeats the same wrong framing. Consider a name like `OrganizationEventsStatsTopNEventsDiscover`, or drop the rename.

`organization_context.member` can be None, and this line runs on every request, including the default path

`enable_advanced` is computed on every request, before the `use_optimized` check, so a request without `optimized_pagination` is affected too. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is typed `RpcOrganizationMember | None` (organizations/services/organization/model.py:346). When the caller is not an org member and not `is_superuser`, `.has_global_access` raises `AttributeError` and the request returns 500. That covers API-key/token auth, where `request.user` is anonymous, and staff. Before this change those callers got the audit log. Fix: check `use_optimized` first and guard the member, e.g. `member = organization_context.member; enable_advanced = is_active_superuser(request) or (member is not None and member.has_global_access)`.

OptimizedCursorPaginator copies the integer `Paginator` key logic but is used with a datetime column

`get_item_key` and `value_from_cursor` are copied from `Paginator` (lines 222-227). The endpoint uses this class with `order_by="-datetime"` (organization_auditlogs.py:80), so `getattr(item, 'datetime')` returns a `datetime`. `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on it raises `TypeError` when `build_cursor` computes the next/prev cursors (cursors.py:258-265). As a result, every opted-in request that has results returns 500. On a follow-up cursor, `value_from_cursor` also returns the raw millisecond integer, which `build_queryset` compares against a timestamp column (`datetime <= 1700000000000`, line 122-126). Fix: subclass `DateTimePaginator`, or reuse its `get_item_key`/`value_from_cursor` (lines 230-241), instead of the integer versions.

Negative offsets don't work: Django querysets reject negative slicing, so this branch always returns 500

The comment says "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically". It doesn't: `QuerySet.__getitem__` raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`. `paginate` only turns `BadPaginationError` into a 400 (base.py:540-541), so any cursor like `0:-5:0` sent with `optimized_pagination=true` returns an unhandled 500. The comment on line 878 says the goal is to "access data beyond normal pagination bounds", which a paginator should never do; the org filter is the only thing that keeps this from being a scoping problem. Remove the branch, or reject negative offsets with `BadPaginationError`.

Shared BasePaginator still passes negative offsets through on prev cursors, and the comment calls it safe

This change affects every `BasePaginator` subclass (`Paginator`, `DateTimePaginator`, …). It clamps negative offsets for next cursors only. A prev cursor (`is_prev=1`) with a negative offset still reaches `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, and Django raises `ValueError` → 500. That was also the behaviour before the change, so it is not a regression. But the comment "the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions" is false, and the asymmetric clamp looks deliberate when it isn't. Rejecting `offset < 0` with `BadPaginationError` would give a 400 for both directions. Line 192 also still compares against `offset` rather than `start_offset`.

Uses the raw `is_superuser` flag instead of `is_active_superuser(request)`

This endpoint's permission class checks `is_active_superuser(request)` (api/bases/organization.py:124), which requires an active superuser session. The raw `request.user.is_superuser` flag is true even without one, so this gate is weaker than the rest of the endpoint. The optimized path only reads the same org-filtered queryset, so no extra data is exposed today. Still, it should use the same check, especially since the paginator comments describe reaching data "beyond normal pagination bounds".

Comment claims negative offset support that no code here adds

The only change in this file is a comment. It says negative offsets are allowed "for efficient reverse pagination", but `int(offset)` was already the code before. Negative offsets also fail downstream in Django slicing (see paginator.py:877). Drop the comment, or validate `offset >= 0` here.

No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the `optimized_pagination` parameter

Nothing in the change exercises the new paginator or the new endpoint branch. A single test calling the audit-log endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true` as an owner would have hit the `TypeError` in `get_item_key`. A test using an API key / non-member caller would have hit the `member is None` crash on the default path.

TotalDocs iterates b.cache without cacheMu, and init now calls it while the watch goroutine can be writing the map

`TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` with no lock (bleve.go:144-153). `BuildIndex` writes the map under `cacheMu.Lock()` (bleve.go:137-139). The new log line at search.go:216 calls `s.search.TotalDocs()` after the watch goroutine has already started (search.go:202-213). For every event, that goroutine calls `getOrCreateIndex`, and on a cache miss it runs `BuildIndex`, which writes `b.cache`. If an event for a namespace/resource with no index yet arrives right as init finishes, the map is iterated and written at the same moment. Go aborts the process with `concurrent map iteration and map write`, so storage startup crashes. The metrics collector (bleve_index_metrics.go:96) has the same unlocked read; until now it was the only caller. Fix: take `b.cacheMu.RLock()`/`RUnlock()` in `TotalDocs`.

Parallel init workers share the outer `err` (and `totalBatchesIndexed`), and they now really do run in parallel

Every `group.Go` closure assigns to the `err` declared at line 181 (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and then returns it. It also increments the shared `totalBatchesIndexed` without synchronization (line 189). Before this PR, `BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for the whole build, so the workers effectively ran one at a time. With the lock now taken only around the map write (bleve.go:137-139), `WorkerThreads` > 1 runs builds at the same time. One worker can overwrite another's non-nil `err` with nil between the assignment and the `return err`. `group.Wait()` then returns nil, and init reports success with an index missing; that index is only built later, on first lazy access. The span attribute count at line 199 also becomes unreliable. Fix: declare the error inside the closure (`_, _, err := s.build(...)`) and use an atomic counter or a mutex for `totalBatchesIndexed`.

Postgres skip probably hides a test config bug that eager Init now exposes

Before this PR, `server.Init` (and with it `backend.Init`, i.e. the DB connection) ran lazily on the first request, so this test passed without the storage server ever touching the resource DB. Now `NewResourceServer` calls `s.Init` (server.go:258), so `sql/service.go:113` connects at module start. For postgres, `addStorageServerToConfig` hardcodes `db_host = "localhost"` (line 76). The mysql branch's comment (line 81) says localhost does not work in Drone, and that branch parses the host from the connection string. That fits "fails in Drone, works locally". Parsing the postgres host from `connection_string` the same way would likely let the test run again instead of being skipped.

Stop's `initErr` no longer blocks requests after shutdown

`Stop` still sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping"/"service is stopped" (lines 321, 328, 339). Before, those values reached clients because every handler called `s.Init(ctx)`, which returns `s.initErr`. Now that those calls are gone, nothing reads `initErr` after construction. After `Stop`, Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Search, and `IsHealthy` (which feeds the gRPC health service, health.go:35), keep being served as normal, and the writes to `initErr` are dead. If refusing requests after shutdown matters, add an explicit stopped check (e.g. an atomic flag) to the handlers or at least to `IsHealthy`. Otherwise, remove the `initErr` writes in `Stop`.

Init failure is logged twice, and the server context is not cancelled on that path

`Init` already logs "error initializing resource server" (line 314), and `NewResourceServer` logs the same message again (line 260). On this error path the constructor also returns without calling `s.cancel()` for the context made at line 229. If `initWatcher` fails after `search.init` succeeded, the search watch goroutine started at search.go:207 keeps running on `context.Background()`.

MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and can't be instantiated

`MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler` and its body is just `pass`. That leaves four abstract members unimplemented: `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values` (processors/detector.py:142-164) and the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data` (processors/detector.py:166-170). `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler` points at this class (grouptype.py:27), and `Detector.detector_handler` instantiates it with `group_type.detector_handler(self)` (models/detector.py:86). So for any Detector with `type="metric_alert_fire"`, reading `detector.detector_handler` now raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class`. Before this change the handler returned `[]` from `evaluate`. Nothing in `src/` calls `process_detectors` today, so this doesn't break anything yet. It will break `process_detectors` as soon as a metric-alert detector reaches it. Either keep stub implementations for now (`counter_names = []`, and the getters returning 0 and `{}`, plus a `build_occurrence_and_event_data` that raises `NotImplementedError`), or don't register the handler on `MetricAlertFire` until it exists. The TODO on line 10 ("will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction") is also out of date now.

Occurrence assertions only compare a hard-coded id, so fingerprint, priority and type go unchecked

Strategy close() shuts down the factory's shared queue pool; after the first rebalance every message is dropped and its offset committed

The factory builds one `FixedQueuePool` in `__init__` (result_consumer.py:133-137) and passes that same object to every strategy `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` returns (result_consumer.py:254-259). Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the strategy on every partition revocation, and both end in `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (queue_consumer.py:338, 345). The factory's `queue_pool` is not reset (only `factory.shutdown()` sets it to None, result_consumer.py:183-185), so the next `create_with_partitions` passes the `assert` and gets a strategy backed by a dead pool. In Python 3.13, `Queue.put` on a shut-down queue raises `queue.ShutDown`, an `Exception` subclass. `submit` catches it (queue_consumer.py:317-325), marks the offset added and completed, and the commit loop commits it. Work queues are unbounded, so the claimed backpressure doesn't exist and memory grows without limit

When processing is slower than consumption, arroyo keeps polling and every message (plus its full `Message` held in `WorkItem.message`) piles up in memory until the process is OOM-killed. `all_offsets` in the tracker grows the same way. The class docstring says the opposite: "Natural backpressure when queues fill up" (line 253). Is arroyo's `Commit` callable safe to call from a background thread?

`_commit_loop` runs on its own daemon thread and calls `commit_function`, which calls the arroyo `Commit` passed to `create_with_partitions` (result_consumer.py:249-252). Every other mode commits through `CommitOffsets` from the processor's poll thread (result_consumer.py:217, 224, 236). I couldn't read arroyo's `StreamProcessor` here. Shutdown can block the rebalance for 5s + 5s × num_queues, and items finished after the commit thread stops are never committed

`close()` joins the commit thread for up to 5s, then `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` joins each worker one after another with `timeout=5.0`. Nothing bounds the whole operation, so the worst case is 5 + 5 × 20 = 105s with the default queue count. With `shutdown(immediate=False)` the workers also drain unbounded queues first. All of this runs on the consumer thread during revocation and can exceed `max.poll.interval.ms`. Also, the commit thread is stopped before the drain, so the offsets of drained items are never committed, and the items are processed again by the next owner. Consider one overall deadline across the joins, and a final commit after the drain.

Commit calculation assumes Kafka offsets are contiguous

`get_committable_offsets` stops at the first offset number that was never added. Kafka offsets can have gaps (transaction control markers, compacted topics). Messages behind such a gap would never be committed and `all_offsets` would grow forever. If the uptime results topic can't have gaps, a comment saying so would help. Otherwise, use the sorted set of seen offsets instead of `range()`.

`test_stats_reporting` races the worker threads

`test_preserves_order_within_group` doesn't check order

Each result opens two nested Sentry transactions

The worker wraps `result_processor` in `start_transaction`, and `ResultProcessor.__call__` opens its own transaction (result_consumer.py:48-51). The serial and batched modes only use the inner one. Error-handling test asserts that nothing is committed, which contradicts its docstring and only holds because of timing

The docstring says errors in processing "don't block offset commits for other messages". The assertion checks the opposite: `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`.

Graceful-shutdown test asserts only something `shutdown()` always sets

The pipeline `execute()` at buffer.py:201 raises on the error, so `process_batch` fails and the consumer crash-loops until every old key expires. Segments still stored as SETs can never be flushed, so they are lost. A rolling deploy makes it worse: old consumers keep `SADD`ing to the same keys while new ones `ZADD`. You need a migration plan, e.g. a new key prefix or version so old and new keys never collide, plus a drain step for the old format.

OptimizedCursorPaginator can't paginate a datetime key, so the audit-log optimized path returns 500

The endpoint uses this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"` (organization_auditlogs.py:79-80). `get_item_key` runs `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly on the `datetime` attribute, which raises TypeError. Denial cache key ignores identity type, so anonymous and renderer share denials

`userPermDenialCacheKey` is built from `checkReq.UserUID` (service.go:116) and does not include the identity type. Both anonymous and render-service identities use UID "0" (`pkg/services/user/identity.go:296-298`). OAuth `state` is a constant, not a per-session secret

`pipeline.signature` is `md5_text(*pipe_ids)` over the view class names (src/sentry/pipeline/base.py:132-133). Scenario: org X is disabled. An admin sets its public IDP to `hideOnLogin=true`, `linkOnly=true`, or makes it non-public. `original` fails the predicate because the wrapper says it is disabled. `updated` fails because it is now hidden. Legacy writes now run in a goroutine on the request context and their failures are never logged

Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection (lines 50, 108, 134, 161) now write to legacy storage in a goroutine. The goroutine's context comes from the request `ctx` through `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. That timeout only puts an upper limit on the wait. It does nothing about the parent being cancelled, and net/http cancels the request context as soon as the handler returns, which is right after `return created, err`. So the legacy write races against its own cancellation. When it loses, or fails for any other reason, the code only records a duration histogram with `isError=true`. Nothing is logged. The old synchronous code at least ran to completion and logged `unable to create object in legacy storage`. In mode 3, legacy is the copy you fall back to if you roll back to mode 2 or 1, so any lost write there is silent data loss on rollback. Fix: run the goroutine on `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` with the timeout on top, and call `log.Error` on `errObjectSt`/`err`. Mode 1 has the same pattern (dualwriter_mode1.go:54), but there the async side is the non-authoritative store.

A rejected device is cached, so its next request gets in and the limit does nothing

`tagDeviceUI` writes the device key to `localCache` (line 87) before it calls `CreateOrUpdateDevice` (line 93), and it does not remove the key on error. Take a new device that arrives once the limit is reached: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, and `Anonymous.Authenticate` rejects that one request (`client.go:45-46`). For the next 29 minutes, every other request from that device on the same instance hits the cache at lines 83-84. `TagDevice` then returns nil and the device is authenticated anonymously. A page load sends many parallel requests, so in practice only the first one fails. The device never gets a DB row, so it is not counted either, and any number of devices over the limit can use the instance. Fix: only set the cache entry after `CreateOrUpdateDevice` succeeds, or delete the key when it returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`.

Count-then-insert is not atomic, so concurrent new devices can go over the limit

The `CountDevices` check (line 110) and the insert (lines 149-153) run in separate sessions with no lock. With N instances, or concurrent first requests from different devices, all of them can read `count < limit` and insert. If the limit is a soft cap this is acceptable, but consider documenting that. If it must be a hard cap, use one conditional statement or a transaction.

Device tagging moved from a background goroutine onto the request path for every deployment

Before this change, `TagDevice` ran in a goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout. Now it runs synchronously inside `Authenticate` with the request context, even when `device_limit` is 0. Each uncached anonymous request now waits for the upsert. When a limit is set, it also waits for a `COUNT(*)` over `anon_device` (`database.go:110`). A request cancelled by the client now also cancels the tag write. To keep the old latency for the default configuration, you could tag synchronously only when `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit > 0`.

`TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only checks that a second, new device is rejected. The `updateDevice` path, which lets an existing device refresh while the limit is reached, has no test. Neither does the auth-level behaviour, where `Authenticate` returns an error and a repeat request should still be rejected; that missing test would have caught the cache bypass in `impl.go`. The second device is also named `"keep"` even though it is the one being rejected, which is misleading.

`device_limit` is read from `[auth.anonymous]`, but a repository search finds no other mention of it, in `conf/defaults.ini`, `conf/sample.ini` or the docs. Operators cannot find the setting, and nothing tells them what happens at the limit: new anonymous devices are rejected and existing ones keep working for 30 days after their last activity.

Field type is inferred as `undefined`, while the backend always sends a number

`anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` with no annotation makes the class field's type `undefined`, so `config.anonymousDeviceLimit` cannot be used as a number without a cast. The backend DTO is a plain `int64` (`frontend_settings.go:195`), so the value is `0` when no limit is set, never `undefined`. Consider `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;`, or typing it as `number` with default `0`. Nothing in the frontend reads this field yet.

Fallback chain depends on the site's default_locale, but the process-wide translation cache key doesn't include it

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` builds the chain from `SiteSetting.default_locale`, which is set per site in multisite and can be changed by an admin. The cached `I18n.translate` in `lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb:71-76` stores results in one process-wide LRU keyed only by `"#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"`. Suppose a key is missing in the user's locale (say `ja`). The first site to translate it caches the string from *its* fallback locale (e.g. `fr`). Every other site on the same process then gets that `fr` string for `ja` users, even if its own default is `de`. Changing `default_locale` in admin also leaves stale fallback strings cached until the process restarts. Nothing errors or logs; users just see text in the wrong language. Fix: add `SiteSetting.default_locale` (or the joined fallback chain) to the cache key `k`.

Fallback locales are only loaded for web requests, not in Sidekiq jobs

The patched I18n loads locale files lazily, and only for `config.locale` (`lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb:68`). The Fallbacks backend looks keys up in the fallback locales without loading them. `ensure_loaded!` is called only from `ApplicationController#set_locale` (`app/controllers/application_controller.rb:159`). Jobs set `I18n.locale = SiteSetting.default_locale` (`app/jobs/base.rb:151`) and never call it. `PostAlerter` also switches to `user.effective_locale` (`app/services/post_alerter.rb:138`) without loading the fallbacks. So in a Sidekiq process whose default locale is not `en`, `:en` may never be loaded. A key missing in the user's or site's locale then renders as `translation missing: …` instead of the English string, and that result is cached. This affects emails and notifications, which are built in jobs. Fix: call `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` after the locale is set in `Jobs::Base` (and in `PostAlerter`'s `with_locale` block). Alternatively, load lazily inside the lookup.

No specs for the new fallback chain

The change turns fallbacks on in every environment, including test and development; before, they were on only in production and profile. No spec covers the user → site default → `en` order, deduplication when they are the same, or `ensure_loaded!`. A spec that stubs `SiteSetting.default_locale` and checks a key present only in `en` or only in the site locale would protect this behaviour, including the multisite cache issue.

Test asks for fruit 2 but asserts fruit 1's colors

`sed -i ''` is BSD sed syntax. Run from the repo root (`scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh`), it creates or edits a `.env` one level above the repository. Resolve the path from `$(dirname "$0")` and use a portable in-place edit. Separately, `cleanup` always runs `exit 0`, so the failure branches (lines 49 and 58) report success to the caller.

Working-hours check rejects a slot that falls outside any one entry for that day

The `find` returns true, which rejects the slot, as soon as one working-hours entry whose `days` includes the slot's UTC weekday doesn't contain it. The slot should only be rejected when no entry contains it. `getWorkingHours` regularly produces several entries per day: split shifts, plus the overflow piece it pushes with shifted `days` when local hours cross UTC midnight (`packages/lib/availability.ts:92-121`).

Concrete case: an organizer in UTC-8 who works Mon–Fri 9:00–17:00 gets two entries:
- Mon–Fri 1020–1439
- Tue–Sat 0–60

A Tuesday 00:00 UTC slot (Monday 16:00 local) matches the first entry's day, 0 < 1020, so it is dropped. A split schedule (9–12 and 13–17) loses every afternoon slot the same way. Fixed hosts and round-robin hosts both hit this (lines 488-493 and 513-518).

These slots disappear silently. Fix: invert the check so the slot is kept when `workingHours.some(wh => wh.days.includes(day) && start >= wh.startTime && end <= wh.endTime)`.

Override check rejects slots in the second time range of a multi-range override

Same pattern as the working-hours check. A date override can hold several ranges for one date: `getUserAvailability` maps each availability row with a `date` into its own `{start,end}` (`packages/core/getUserAvailability.ts:215-224`). For a slot inside the second range, the first range on the same date matches the date test, and `slotStartTime.isAfter(range1.end)` returns true. `find` then makes the function return false at line 130, so the valid slot is removed.

Fix: compute whether the slot lies inside some override range for that date (`some(...)`), and reject it only when override ranges exist for the date and none contains it.

Override date is matched on its UTC day, not the organizer's day

After the shift, `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset)` is the real UTC instant, and the code compares its UTC calendar day with the slot's UTC day. Take an organizer in UTC+10 with an override from 09:00 to 17:00 (23:00 the previous UTC day to 07:00 UTC). The override's UTC day is D-1, so a 03:00 UTC slot on D doesn't match it. `dateOverrideExist` stays false and the slot falls through to the regular working-hours check. If the override was meant to open a day that is normally off, that override slot is rejected. Compare dates in the organizer's time zone, or check the slot against the override's start/end interval directly.

`===` between two Dayjs objects is always false

`dayjs(a) === dayjs(b)` compares two freshly created object references, so this is never true. The "override with start == end (unavailable all day)" case is never handled here. A slot starting exactly at the zero-length override's instant passes both later checks and is treated as available. Use `.isSame(...)`.

`end` is computed from the slot start, so the slot end is never checked

`end` duplicates `start` (both use `slotStartTime`), so `end > workingHour.endTime` only re-tests the start. A slot that starts inside working hours but runs past their end is accepted. Compute `end` from `slotEndTime`, keeping in mind that the end can land on the next UTC day.

Shifted override minutes wrap past midnight and put slots on the wrong day

`startTime` and `endTime` are taken from `.hour()*60 + .minute()` after the time-zone shift, so they wrap modulo 24h. If the invitee offset pushes the override across midnight, the window breaks. Example: organizer in UTC, override 20:00–23:00, invitee +6 gives 02:00–05:00. That window is still attached to `startOfInviteeDay` of the override's original date (`buildSlots` at line 248), so its slots appear about 24h early. A range that straddles midnight (22:00–02:00) gets `endTime < startTime` and produces no slots. Keep the minute offset relative to the invitee day (allowing values below 0 or of 1440 and above, then splitting), instead of taking the clock hour.

New test doesn't exercise the failure modes this change introduces

The added case reuses the +5:30 day window (`T18:30Z`) for a +6:00 invitee and a single-range override. No test has a multi-range override, a split or UTC-midnight-crossing working-hours schedule, or a round-robin host. Those are the paths the new `checkIfIsAvailable` logic changes, and it currently breaks them (see findings at lines 106 and 139). Consider adding cases for each.

Reminders are permanently deleted after two failed attempts, about 30 minutes apart, including for a temporary SMS lock

`twilio.scheduleSMS` returns `undefined` when the user or team is in `SMSLockState.LOCKED` (twilioProvider.ts:90-95). The new `else` branch counts that as a failure and increments `retryCount`. The catch block at lines 189-197 does the same for any thrown error. That includes `checkSMSRateLimit` throwing once the 250-per-30-day `smsMonth` limit is hit (twilioProvider.ts:97-102, rateLimit.ts:91-95), and any transient Twilio error. The cron runs every 15 minutes (.github/workflows/cron-scheduleSMSReminders.yml:8). So after two runs `retryCount` is 2, and the deleteMany at lines 38-42 removes the row on the third run. This can happen to a reminder whose `scheduledDate` is still up to 7 days away. Before this change, those reminders stayed `scheduled: false` and were picked up again once the lock was lifted or the limit window moved on. Now they are deleted with only a `console.log` in the thrown case, and with no log at all in the locked case. The organizer is not told and the attendee never gets the reminder. Suggested fix: don't count the locked state (the `undefined` return) as a retry. Either give up only when the reminder can no longer be scheduled (`scheduledDate` too close), or space retries out and allow many more of them than two runs, which cover just 30 minutes.

An unguarded `update` in the catch block can abort the whole cron run

Before this change the catch block only logged, so one bad reminder never stopped the loop. Now it runs `prisma.workflowReminder.update({ where: { id } })` without its own try/catch. Prisma's `update` throws (P2025) when the row is gone. Rows are hard-deleted when a booking is cancelled or rescheduled (`deleteScheduledSMSReminder`, smsReminderManager.ts:251-255). That deletion can happen while this loop is awaiting Twilio or other DB calls for earlier reminders. In that case the update at line 179 or 169 throws inside `try`, the catch's own update throws again, and the error leaves `handler`. Every reminder after it in `unscheduledReminders` is skipped for this run. Twilio only accepts a `sendAt` at least 15 minutes ahead, so a reminder due just after this run may miss its slot entirely. Suggested fix: wrap the retry bookkeeping in its own try/catch, or use `updateMany({ where: { id } })`, which does not throw when the row is missing.

The `retryCount` delete condition is not limited to SMS reminders

The second branch of the `OR` has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`. This SMS cron therefore deletes EMAIL and WHATSAPP `WorkflowReminder` rows whose `retryCount` is greater than 1. Today only this file writes `retryCount`, so nothing else is affected yet. Once the email or WhatsApp crons start counting retries in the same column, the SMS cron will delete their rows, possibly before those crons get their own attempt. Consider adding `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` to that branch.

Only the first branch of getBaseConditions can run

`getAuthorizationConditions()` always returns a `Prisma.Sql` object (lines 83-88, 125-143), and an object is always truthy. So `authConditions` is never falsy, and the `else if (filterConditions)` and `else return NOTHING_CONDITION` branches (lines 76-79) can never run. They also suggest that a filter-only result can skip authorization, which can't happen today and would be risky if it ever did. Suggest simplifying to `return filterConditions ? Prisma.sql`(${authConditions}) AND (${filterConditions})` : authConditions;`.

Org and team SQL is never run against the database

This test is now the only one that runs the generated SQL against Postgres, and it only covers `scope: "user"` with an eventTypeId filter. The org and team tests (lines 278-346) only check that the `Prisma.sql` objects are structurally equal. So the new `"teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})` / `"userId" = ANY(${userIds})` array bindings (insightsBooking.ts:164, 168, 197, 201) are never shown to work: correct parameter typing, and the right rows coming back. A `$queryRaw` test for team and org scope, with one team booking and one personal booking, would cover the part of this rewrite most likely to break. The removed caching tests also leave `getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions` memoization (lines 83-95) untested, and that code is still there.

Constructor type no longer requires teamId for team scope

`InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` makes `teamId` optional for every scope. Before, the constructor took the discriminated union. Now a caller can pass `{ scope: "team", userId, orgId }` without a compile error. At runtime the zod parse (line 62) fails, so the service quietly returns `1=0` and shows no data instead of a type error. That fails closed, so it's safe, but the mistake moves from compile time to a silent empty result. Keep the discriminated union, or document why the looser type is needed. No caller in the repository needs it today: the only constructor calls are in the integration test.

Google credential key is saved as the zod SafeParse wrapper, which breaks every Google Calendar credential after its first refresh

`parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the `safeParse` result (`{ success, data }`), not the parsed token (parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:29). Line 97 assigns that wrapper to `key` and writes it to the credential at line 100. This happens even when credential sharing is off. The next time a `GoogleCalendarService` is built, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` at line 75 gets `{ success: true, data: {...} }` and throws, so the calendar stops working for every user whose token gets refreshed. Fix: use `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...).data` when you write the key.

This file never imports `prisma` (grep finds only line 96). It type-checks only because `globalThis.prisma` is declared globally. `packages/prisma/index.ts:58-60` assigns `globalThis.prisma` only when `NODE_ENV !== "production"`. Salesforce refreshes its token on every client creation, skips the sync endpoint, and keeps the stale access token

`getClient` now POSTs to Salesforce's token endpoint every time a service is constructed. It does not check expiry first, and it does not go through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so self-hosters with sync enabled still hit Salesforce directly with their own consumer secret. The new token is stored (line 98), but the `jsforce.Connection` is still built with the old `credentialKey.access_token` and `instance_url` (lines 105-106), so the refresh has no effect on the connection that is returned. Also, if the refresh fails, construction now fails (line 86), where before jsforce refreshed lazily. Suggested fix: send the call through `refreshOAuthTokens` and build the connection from `accessTokenParsed.data`.

In sync mode the helper returns a raw fetch `Response`, but several callers expect an SDK or axios result

With sync enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the `fetch` Response object. The fetch-based callers (Lark, Office365, Webex, Zoom) run it through `handleErrorsJson` and similar handlers, so they work. The other callers do not:

- HubSpot treats the Response as a `HubspotToken` and writes it as the credential key (hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts:192-198).
- Zoho Bigin and Zoho CRM read `tokenInfo.data.error` (zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts:96, and the zohocrm equivalent), which is undefined.

In short, the feature this PR adds is broken for those four apps. The helper also never checks `response.ok`. Fix: have the helper return parsed JSON in a shape callers can rely on, or adapt each caller.

The minimum token schema's computed keys both become "[object Object]", so the schema strips expiry fields

`[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal key `"[object Object]"`. The second overwrites the first, so the schema is `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]"?: unknown }`. `z.object` strips unknown keys, so in sync mode `expires_in`, `expiry_date` and every other field is dropped. For example, Zoom then computes `Date.now() + undefined * 1000 = NaN` as `expiry_date` (zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:122) and stores the placeholder `"refresh_token"` as its refresh token (line 120). Use `z.object({ access_token: z.string() }).passthrough()` instead, and validate an expiry field explicitly.

The placeholder `refresh_token = "refresh_token"` can overwrite a real refresh token

When a refresh response has no `refresh_token`, the helper inserts the string literal "refresh_token". It does this in non-sync mode too. Office365 spreads `tokenResponse.data` over the stored credentials (office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:264), and Zoom assigns `newTokens.refresh_token` (zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:120). In both cases, a provider response without a refresh token replaces the real stored token with the placeholder. The next refresh then fails, and nothing tells the user why. Zoho Bigin sends the credential id as the Cal.com user id

`refreshAccessToken(credentialId, credentialKey)` passes `credentialId` as the `userId` argument of `refreshOAuthTokens`. The sync endpoint therefore receives `calcomUserId=<credential id>`, and with it the wrong user's tokens or none at all. The user-only check (`&& userId`) is also bypassed for team credentials. Pass the credential's `userId` instead.

`appStoreMetadata` is keyed by directory name but the lookup uses the app slug

`appStoreMetadata` is keyed by app directory (apps.metadata.generated.ts:98 `googlecalendar`, :146 `zoomvideo`), but `app.slug` is the slug (`google-calendar`, `zoom`, `lark-calendar`; see googlecalendar/_metadata.ts:17, zoomvideo/_metadata.ts:16). The other callers send the slug (`google-calendar`, `lark-calendar`, `msteams`), but Zoom sends its directory name, while `zoomvideo/_metadata.ts:16` declares `slug: "zoom"`. The parent application's sync endpoint and the webhook's `appSlug` therefore use different identifiers for Zoom.

Webhook secret check is not constant-time, and malformed input returns a 500

The secret is compared with `!==` instead of `crypto.timingSafeEqual`. If `parse` (line 31) or the decrypt-and-`JSON.parse` step (lines 57-59) throws on a malformed body or wrong key, the error goes unhandled and the endpoint returns 500 instead of 400. Consider `timingSafeEqual` together with `safeParse` and a try/catch around decryption.

The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` contains only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug`. It carries no secret or signature, so the parent application cannot tell that the caller is Cal.com, and anyone who can reach that endpoint can ask it for a user's access token. Consider sending `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` in a header, the same way the inbound webhook requires it.

`tokenResponse.success &&` is dead code now that the helper throws, and the MS error log was removed

`parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws when `success` is false (parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:21-23), so the `success` guards here, at zoomvideo VideoApiAdapter.ts:108 and at salesforce CalendarService.ts:92 can never be false. The old code logged the zod error and Microsoft's response. The new throw message has neither, which makes Outlook refresh failures harder to diagnose.

One failed SendGrid cancel stops every later cancellation in the run

The whole loop sits inside one try (lines 53-77), and each `client.request` is awaited in order. If one cancel throws (for example a bad or already-handled batch_id), two things happen:

1. Every reminder after it in `remindersToCancel` is skipped for this run.
2. None of the deletes queued so far run. Prisma promises are lazy and only run at the `Promise.all` on line 74, which is never reached.

The next cron run fetches the same rows in the same order and fails at the same place. This repeats until line 34 removes the bad row once its `scheduledDate` has passed. By then the reminders behind it have reached their send time, so their emails go out for bookings that were cancelled or rescheduled. Only a `console.log` records it.

Reminder cancellation is no longer awaited before the handler returns

Before, the reminder `deleteMany` calls were added to `prismaPromises` and awaited (old lines ~505-508). Now `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are async calls nobody awaits inside `forEach`. Line 495 no longer waits for any reminder work.

The same fire-and-forget pattern appears in bookings.tsx:489-493, handleNewBooking.ts:966-972 and workflows.tsx:212-218/376-382/519-525/574-580.

Fix: collect the promises (`map` instead of `forEach`) and `await Promise.all(...)` them.

try/catch around the non-awaited reminder calls catches nothing

The `forEach` callbacks start async calls without awaiting them, so a rejection never reaches this `catch`. Both callees already catch internally (emailReminderManager.ts:233, smsReminderManager.ts:187), so the `log.error` at line 974 can never run. If you await the calls (see the finding on handleCancelBooking), the try/catch starts doing something; otherwise remove it.

`packages/config/eslint-preset.js:35-43` sets `@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-imports` to "error" with `prefer: "type-imports"`.

The handler lowercases `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS` (line 71) but compares it to the raw `guest` (line 77). `Blocked@Example.com`, or a `+alias` of it, gets past the blacklist. Emails are keyed on the raw `guests` input, not on the guests actually added

`sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` passes the unfiltered input. packages/ui file imports from its own barrel

The "copied" toast shows even when the clipboard write fails

The new tests only click the download, copy and close buttons. Every app module still loads as soon as index.ts is evaluated

isAccessTokenId never checks the grant shortcut: wrong offset and inverted comparison

The encoded prefix is `<session 2><tokenType 2><grant 2>` (DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.java:78-81), so the grant shortcut is `substring(4, 6)`. `substring(3, 5)` reads the last char of the token type and the first char of the grant (e.g. `onrtac` → `ta`). The check is also inverted: it returns `false` when the slice *equals* the expected shortcut. Together this means the matcher accepts any token id of the form `xxxxxx:<uuid>`, whatever grant is encoded. So `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken` and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` assert nothing about the grant. If you only fix the offset, every one of these assertions fails, because the inverted check is still there. Fix: `if (items[0].length() != 6 || !items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. The length check also stops an id with a short prefix from throwing StringIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of returning a mismatch.

client_credentials, UMA and legacy token-exchange tokens are encoded with grant 'na'

ClientCredentialsGrantType builds its token with `tokenManager.responseBuilder(...).generateAccessToken()` (ClientCredentialsGrantType.java:140-141) and never goes through `OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse`, so the attribute is never set. Every service-account token is therefore encoded as `..na:<id>`, even though this factory registers `cc` and the unit test's sample id is `trltcc:1234`. The same applies to the UMA permission grant (`pg`, AuthorizationTokenService.java:358) and the legacy token-exchange path (AbstractTokenExchangeProvider.java:410): neither sets the attribute. Anything that reads the grant back from the jti gets a wrong answer with no error. Set `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, context.getGrantType())` before `generateAccessToken()` in ClientCredentialsGrantType, the same way ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType.java:134 does, and do the same for the other two paths.

The old path always went through `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential`, which deletes any existing local `recovery-authn-codes` credential before it creates the new one (services/.../credential/RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.java:39-40). Removing an exhausted credential does nothing when it comes from user storage

`RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` can now return a credential from the federated storage (`getFederatedCredentialsStream`). `removeStoredCredentialById` only goes to the local store (`getStoreForUser(user).removeStoredCredential`, UserCredentialManager.java:114-117), so a storage credential whose codes are all used is never removed. Test storage accepts any recovery code any number of times, and the test never checks that a code gets used up

With V2 on, deleting a client leaves its per-client FGAP resource and permissions behind

The listener now only runs when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) is on. That keeps `ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled` (ClientPermissionsV2.java:193, which throws UnsupportedOperationException) from running under V2. The trouble is that nothing else removes a V2 per-client resource when its client is deleted. `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` names that resource after the client UUID (AdminPermissionsSchema.java:93-104). `ClientApplicationSynchronizer.removeFromClientPolicies` (ClientApplicationSynchronizer.java:49-75) only deletes the client's own resource server and clears client policies. Users get different treatment: `UserSynchronizer.removeUserResources` cleans up their V2 resources.

So after an admin deletes a client that had a per-client permission (e.g. MANAGE on `myclient`), the resource and the scope permission stay in the admin-permissions client. They point at an id that no longer exists, and no error or log says so. Suggested fix: add V2 cleanup of the client's resource on `ClientRemovedEvent`, the same way users are handled, and a test that deletes a client that has a per-client permission.

Possible NPE when the realm has no "Clients" type resource

`getResourceTypeResource` returns null when the realm has no resource named `Clients` (AdminPermissionsSchema.java:131-133). The result goes straight into `findByResource(server, resource)` and later `resource.getScopes()` with no null check. Could a realm that turned on admin permissions V2 before `CLIENTS` was added to the schema lack this type resource? If so, any admin without manage-clients/view-clients who reaches `canView(client)` would get a 500 instead of a 403. A `resource == null` guard that returns false would rule this out.

canView(client) can run up to four full policy evaluations per client

`canView(client)` calls `canView()`, which evaluates the type resource for VIEW. It then calls `canConfigure` → `canManage` → `hasPermission(client, MANAGE)`, then `hasPermission(client, CONFIGURE)`, and finally `hasPermission(client, VIEW)`. Each call builds a `ResourcePermission` with all of the resource's scopes and evaluates it again, then keeps only one scope. When clients are listed, that happens for every client. One evaluation per resource, with every granted scope checked against it, would give the same answer for a quarter of the work.
